title: The conditional: polite requests, wishes and 'if'
objectives: I can form the conditional from the past form of a verb and the particle 'би', writing 'б' after a vowel and 'би' after a consonant.
I can make polite requests and offers with 'Я б хоті́в...', 'Я б хоті́ла...', 'Ви б хоті́ли...?' and 'Чи не могли́ б ви...?'.
I can tell a real condition with 'якщо́' and the future from an imagined one with 'якби́' and the past form, about the present and about the past.
I can give advice with 'На тво́єму мі́сці я б...' and 'ра́дити', and express wishes and regret with 'Як би я хоті́в...!', 'Якби́...!' and 'шко́да'.
I can explain why 'якби́' is one word and 'як би' two, why 'якби́' is said with [ɡ], and why 'ра́дити' has 'дж' in 'ра́джу'.

vocabulary.note: A particle that makes the conditional together with the past form of a verb. It never changes, because the past form already shows gender and number. It is written 'би' after a consonant and 'б' after a vowel.

It introduces a condition that the speaker presents as unreal: only imagined, or contrary to the facts. It is 'як' and 'би' written as one word, so the verb in its clause is the past form and takes no second 'би'. A real condition takes 'якщо́' instead.

example.target: Якби́ я знав, я б тобі́ сказа́в.
example.source: If I had known, I would have told you.
example.source_literal: If-would I knew, I would to-you told.

vocabulary.note: 'Мрі́ю', 'мрі́єш', 'мрі́ють', like 'чита́ти'. What you dream of follows 'про' with the accusative. It names wishing and imagining while awake, not the dreams of sleep. It has no perfective partner; the perfective 'помрі́яти' means to dream for a while.

example.source: The children are dreaming of the holidays.

vocabulary.note: Something you hope for and would like to come true. Plural 'мрі́ї'.

'Ви́граю', 'ви́граєш'; imperfective partner 'виграва́ти' ('виграва́ю', 'виграва́єш'). What is won is in the accusative: 'ви́грати гро́ші'. A game or a lottery follows 'у' or 'в' with the accusative, as in 'гра́ти у футбо́л': 'ви́грати в лотере́ю'.
Accusative 'лотере́ю', locative 'у лотере́ї'. 'Гра́ти в лотере́ю' is to play the lottery.

example.target: Мій діду́сь ко́жен ти́ждень гра́є в лотере́ю.
example.source: My grandfather plays the lottery every week.
example.source_literal: My grandfather each week plays in lottery.

vocabulary.note: It has the same root as 'бага́то', a lot.
Before the name of a person or a noun for a person it also expresses sympathy, as English 'poor' does: 'Бі́дний Сем!'

example.target: Бі́дний Сем! У ньо́го боли́ть голова́.
example.source: Poor Sam! He has a headache.
example.source_literal: Poor Sam! At him hurts head.

vocabulary.note: Unlike English 'advice', it is countable: 'одна́ пора́да', 'дві пора́ди'. In 'Дя́кую за пора́ду!' (thanks for the advice) the thing you thank someone for follows 'за' with the accusative.

example.source: Olena gave Taras some good advice.

vocabulary.note: 'Ра́джу', 'ра́диш', 'ра́дять': 'д' becomes 'дж' only in the 'я' form. Perfective partner 'пора́дити' ('пора́джу', 'пора́диш'). The person advised is in the dative and what to do is an infinitive. With a thing in the accusative it means to recommend: 'пора́дити готе́ль'.

example.source: I advise you to go by train.

vocabulary.note: 'Мі́сці' is the locative of 'мі́сце', place, after 'на'. To someone you call 'ви' you say 'на ва́шому мі́сці'. 'Тво́єму' is also said 'твоє́му'. The phrase is followed by the conditional.

example.target: На тво́єму мі́сці я б відпочива́в.
example.source: If I were you, I would rest.
example.source_literal: On your place I would rested.

vocabulary.note: It adds what will happen if the advice or request before it is not followed. It also means 'differently': 'Я ду́маю іна́кше.' (I think differently.)

example.target: Візьми́ ку́ртку, іна́кше тобі́ бу́де хо́лодно.
example.source: Take a jacket, otherwise you'll be cold.
example.source_literal: Take jacket, otherwise to-you will-be cold.

vocabulary.note: Like 'тре́ба', it is the predicate of a sentence without a subject. Alone, 'Шко́да!' means 'What a pity!' Followed by 'що' it introduces the fact regretted. With a person in the dative it says who is sorry: 'Мені́ шко́да.' (I'm sorry, literally 'to-me pity').

example.target: Шко́да, що ти не мо́жеш піти́ з на́ми.
example.source: It's a pity you can't come with us.
example.source_literal: Pity, that you not can to-go with us.

vocabulary.note: 'Ві́льний час' is free time, and 'ві́льне мі́сце' a free seat. It does not mean 'free of charge'.
With a word of time in the accusative it says how long something lasts: 'ці́лий день', 'ці́лий ти́ждень', 'ці́лу ніч'. 'Весь день' means the same as 'ці́лий день'.

example.source: Yesterday I worked the whole day.

grammar.title: The conditional: the past form plus би
grammar.explanation:
A mood is the way a verb presents an action: as a fact (the indicative, which covers every tense you have learned so far), as a command (the imperative), or as something that is not real (the conditional). The unit on verbs named these three moods, and this unit teaches the third. The conditional presents an action as imagined, wished for or politely offered, where English says 'I would go' or 'she would like'.

Ukrainian builds the conditional from two pieces:

- the past form of the verb, which agrees with the subject in gender and number: 'пої́хав', 'пої́хала', 'пої́хало', 'пої́хали'
- the particle 'би', which is written 'б' after a vowel

So 'я б пої́хав' means 'I would go', said by a man, and 'я б пої́хала' is the same said by a woman. A particle is a small word that adds a meaning to the sentence and never changes its own form, like 'не' and 'чи'. 'Би' is not a verb: it does not change for person, gender or number. All of that is carried by the past form, exactly as in the past tense: 'я хоті́в би', 'вона́ хоті́ла б', 'ми хоті́ли б', and 'ви хоті́ли б' to one person or to several. 'Могти́' has no '-в' in the masculine ('міг'), as in the past tense, and since 'міг' ends in a consonant it takes 'би': 'міг би'. The word-for-word glosses in this course render the pair as 'would' plus the past, 'I would went', so that you can see the past form inside it.

With 'би' the past form loses its meaning of past time and carries only gender and number, so one form serves for every time:

- 'За́втра я б пої́хав до Льво́ва.' means 'I would go to Lviv tomorrow'.
- 'Учо́ра я б пої́хав до Льво́ва, але́ не було́ квиткі́в.' means 'I would have gone to Lviv yesterday, but there were no tickets'.

English needs two forms, 'would go' and 'would have gone'. Ukrainian uses one and lets the words of time and the situation decide.

'Би' leans on the word before it and is said together with it. It usually stands right after the first stressed word of the clause, which is often the subject pronoun: 'Я б хоті́ла чай.' It may also follow the verb: 'Я хоті́ла б чай.' Both orders are correct, and the first is more common in speech. In a question it follows the question word: 'Що б ти зроби́в?' (What would you do?), where 'що' and 'б' are two words. The negation 'не' stands right before the verb, as always: 'Я б не пої́хала.' (I wouldn't go.)

Verbs of both aspects form the conditional, and the aspect is chosen as in the past. 'Я б чита́в ці́лий день.' (I would read all day) presents a process, and 'Я б прочита́в цю кни́гу.' (I would read this book through) presents one completed result. A reflexive verb keeps '-ся' on the past form: 'Ми б зустріча́лися ча́сто.' (We would meet often.)

grammar.title: Polite requests, offers, advice and wishes
grammar.explanation:
A request in the conditional sounds softer than the same request stated as a fact, because it is presented as only imagined and leaves the listener free to say no. English does the same when it says 'I would like' for 'I want' and 'Could you...?' for 'Can you...?'.

To ask for something politely, a man says 'Я б хоті́в...' and a woman 'Я б хоті́ла...', followed by a noun in the accusative or by an infinitive: 'Я б хоті́ла чай.' (I would like tea), 'Я б хоті́в купи́ти квито́к до Льво́ва.' (I would like to buy a ticket to Lviv). 'Я хо́чу чай.' (I want tea) is correct too and normal among friends; the conditional is more careful.

To ask someone to do something, use 'Чи не могли́ б ви...?' with an infinitive: 'Чи не могли́ б ви мені́ допомогти́?' (Could you help me?), literally 'whether not could would you to-me to-help?'. 'Чи' is the particle that opens a yes or no question. The 'не' does not make the request negative; it only makes it more tentative, and 'Чи могли́ б ви...?' without 'не' is polite too. With 'ти' the past form agrees with the person asked: 'Чи не міг би ти...?' to a man, 'Чи не могла́ б ти...?' to a woman. An offer works the same way: 'Ви б хоті́ли ка́ву?' and 'Чи не хоті́ли б ви ка́ву?' both mean 'Would you like a coffee?'.

Advice is often given as what the speaker would do in the listener's place. There are three common ways to give it:

- 'На тво́єму мі́сці я б...' to someone you call 'ти', and 'На ва́шому мі́сці я б...' to someone you call 'ви', literally 'on your place I would...', in English 'If I were you, I would...'
- 'Ти б кра́ще...' with the past form, literally 'you would better', in English 'you'd better...': 'Ти б кра́ще пої́хав по́їздом.'
- 'Я ра́джу тобі́...' with an infinitive, literally 'I advise to-you', which gives the advice directly, with the person in the dative

A wish for something that is not real is a conditional too:

- 'Як би я хоті́ла жи́ти бі́ля мо́ря!' (How I would love to live by the sea!), literally 'how would I wanted to-live near sea!'. Here 'як' is 'how', as in an exclamation, and 'би' belongs to the verb, so they are two words.
- 'Якби́ ми жили́ бі́ля мо́ря!' (If only we lived by the sea!) is a clause with 'якби́' and nothing after it; the next note teaches 'якби́'.
- 'Було́ б до́бре...' (It would be good...) uses the 'воно́' form 'було́' in a sentence without a subject, as 'Мені́ тре́ба було́...' does: 'Було́ б до́бре пої́хати ра́зом.'

Regret about the real facts is not a conditional. It uses the predicative word 'шко́да', it is a pity, followed by 'що' and the fact: 'Шко́да, що в ме́не нема́є ча́су.' (It's a pity I don't have time.)

grammar.title: Real and unreal conditions: якщо́ and якби́
grammar.explanation:
A condition is a clause that says under what circumstances something else happens. The unit on the future taught real conditions with 'якщо́'. In a real condition the speaker thinks the condition may be met. When it lies in the future, Ukrainian puts both verbs in the future, where English uses the present in the 'if' clause: 'Якщо́ в ме́не бу́де час, я пої́ду до мо́ря.' (If I have time, I will go to the sea, literally 'if at me will-be time, I will-go to sea').

An unreal condition is one the speaker presents as not true: imagined, unlikely or contrary to the facts. English shows it by shifting the tense back: 'If I had time, I would go'. Ukrainian shows it with the conditional in both clauses:

- the 'if' clause opens with 'якби́' and has the past form of the verb
- the other clause has the past form with 'би' or 'б'

'Якби́ в ме́не був час, я б пої́хав до мо́ря.' (If I had time, I would go to the sea, literally 'if-would at me was time, I would went to sea'.) 'Якби́' is 'як' and 'би' fused into one word, so it already carries the particle, and its clause never takes a second 'би'. The verb after 'якби́' agrees with its own subject: 'Якби́ Оле́на була́ тут...', 'Якби́ ми жили́ в Оде́сі...'.

As in every conditional, one form serves for the present and for the past, and the situation decides:

- 'Якби́ ти мені́ подзвони́в, я б тобі́ допомогла́.' can mean 'If you phoned me, I would help you' or 'If you had phoned me, I would have helped you'.
- A word of time settles it: 'Якби́ ти подзвони́в мені́ вчо́ра, я б тобі́ допомогла́.' is about yesterday.

The choice between 'якщо́' and 'якби́' depends on how the speaker presents the condition. 'Якщо́ я ви́граю в лотере́ю, я куплю́ ха́ту.' treats winning as a real possibility, perhaps as a joke, while 'Якби́ я ви́грав у лотере́ю, я б купи́в ха́ту.' only imagines it. The two patterns are kept apart. 'Якщо́' goes with the future, with the present, or with an imperative in the other clause ('Якщо́ ти ві́льний, ході́мо в кіно́.'), while 'якби́' goes only with the past form.

Either clause can come first, and a comma always separates them: 'Я б купи́ла цю су́кню, якби́ вона́ була́ деше́вша.' (I would buy this dress if it were cheaper.) A clause with 'якби́' can also stand alone as a wish, as the previous note showed: 'Якби́ в ме́не був час!' (If only I had time!)

grammar.title: Spelling and sound: б and би, якби́ and як би, ра́джу
grammar.explanation:
The particle has two spellings for the same reason that 'у' and 'в', and 'і' and 'й', have two: Ukrainian prefers an even flow of vowels and consonants. After a word that ends in a vowel it is written 'б', and after a word that ends in a consonant, 'й' included, it is written 'би':

- 'я б', 'ти б', 'вона́ б', 'ми б', 'хоті́ла б', 'могли́ б'
- 'він би', 'Тара́с би', 'Андрі́й би', 'хоті́в би', 'міг би'

Both are said together with the word before them, as if they were its last syllable, and neither is stressed. After a vowel the 'б' closes the syllable: 'хоті́ла б' [xɔˈtʲilɑb]. It stays voiced, as a voiced consonant does at the end of 'хліб'. After a consonant 'би' adds a syllable: in 'хоті́в би' [xɔˈtʲiw bɪ] the 'в' that ends the past form is [w], as in 'чита́в', and in 'міг би' [mʲiɦ bɪ] the 'г' keeps its voiced [ɦ], since Ukrainian does not devoice a consonant at the end of a word.

'Якби́' is one word and 'як би' is two, and they mean different things:

- 'якби́' is the conjunction 'if' for an unreal condition: 'Якби́ я знав...' (If I had known...)
- 'як би' is 'як', how, followed by the particle 'би' that belongs to the verb: 'Як би я хоті́в...!' (How I would love to...!)

A test tells them apart. In 'як би' the particle can move to the verb without changing the meaning ('Як я хоті́в би...!'), while 'якби́' cannot be split. In speech the two sound almost alike. In both, 'к' before the voiced 'б' is said voiced, [ɡ], as 'к' before 'з' is in 'вокза́л': 'якби́' [jɑɡˈbɪ]. The one word 'якби́' is stressed on its last syllable, while in 'як би' the stress falls on 'як'. The same reasoning writes 'що б' as two words in 'Що б ти зроби́в?' (What would you do?), where 'що' is 'what'.

'Ра́дити' has 'дж' in the 'я' form: 'ра́джу', but 'ра́диш', 'ра́дить', 'ра́дять'. In verbs of the second conjugation a 'д' at the end of the stem becomes 'дж' before the ending '-у', as in 'сиді́ти', 'сиджу́' and 'ходи́ти', 'ходжу́'. The perfective 'пора́дити' does the same, 'пора́джу', while the noun 'пора́да' keeps its 'д'. 'Дж' is one sound, [d͡ʒ], as in 'jam': 'ра́джу' [ˈrɑd͡ʒu].

The other new words follow the rules of the alphabet units:

- In 'мрі́я', 'мрі́ю' and 'мрі́яти' the 'р' is soft before 'і', and 'я' and 'ю' after the vowel 'і' are [jɑ] and [ju]: 'мрі́я' [ˈmrʲijɑ].
- In 'лотере́я' [lɔtɛˈrɛjɑ] the 'т' and 'р' are hard before 'е', the 'я' after a vowel is [jɑ], and the unstressed 'е' of 'те' leans a little toward 'и'.
- A perfective verb with the prefix 'ви-' is stressed on the prefix in every form: 'ви́грати', 'ви́граю', 'ви́грав'. Its imperfective partner 'виграва́ти' is stressed on '-ва́-' in every form ('виграва́ю', 'виграва́є'), so the two verbs of the pair differ in stress.
- In 'ві́льний' [ˈʋʲilʲnɪj] the soft sign makes the 'л' soft before 'н'.
- In 'ці́лий' [ˈt͡sʲilɪj] the 'ц' is soft before 'і'.
- 'Ха́рків' becomes 'до Ха́ркова': the 'і' of the closed last syllable becomes 'о' when an ending opens the syllable, as in 'Львів', 'Льво́ва'.

culture.title: A plane called 'Мрі́я', and when to be careful
culture.text:
The word 'мрі́я' is also the name of a famous airplane. The An-225 'Мрі́я' was a cargo plane designed by the Antonov company in Kyiv. It first flew in 1988, only one was ever completed, and it was the heaviest airplane ever built, with six engines and wings eighty-eight meters across. It carried loads that no other plane could take, and crowds came to airports around the world to watch it land. In February 2022, at the start of Russia's full-scale invasion, it was destroyed at the airfield of Hostomel near Kyiv. For many Ukrainians the lost 'Мрі́я' became a symbol, and many hope that a new one will be built.

In everyday life a request in a shop or a café is usually an imperative with 'будь ла́ска', and it is perfectly polite: 'Да́йте, будь ла́ска, ка́ву.' A question with 'мо́жна' is just as common: 'Мо́жна раху́нок?' The conditional is the more careful choice, and Ukrainians use it in these situations:

- with a stranger in the street: 'Чи не могли́ б ви сказа́ти, де по́шта?'
- when they ask a real favor, something that costs the other person time or trouble
- in offices and on the phone with people they do not know

Among friends the same request is simpler: 'Мо́жеш мені́ допомогти́?' or 'Допоможи́, будь ла́ска.'

Ukrainians give advice readily, and older relatives give it whether or not you ask. 'На тво́єму мі́сці я б...' is the friendly way to do it, because it presents the advice as the speaker's own choice and leaves the decision to the listener.

exercises.explanation: A man says 'хоті́в' and a woman 'хоті́ла'. The particle is 'б' after a vowel and 'би' after a consonant. 'Ча́ю', the genitive, is also correct: with a substance it names an amount, some tea, as it does after 'бага́то'.

exercises.prompt_source: If it were warm, we would go for a walk.
answers: Якби́ було́ те́пло, ми б гуля́ли.

exercises.explanation: An unreal condition: 'якби́' with the past form 'було́', and the past form with 'б' in the other clause.

exercises.explanation: The polite request is 'Чи не могли́ б ви...?' with an infinitive, and 'подзвони́ти' takes the person phoned in the dative, 'мені́'.

exercises.prompt_source: If you are free, phone me. (to a friend)
answers: Якщо́ ти ві́льний, подзвони́ мені́.
Якщо́ ти ві́льна, подзвони́ мені́.

exercises.explanation: The condition is real, so it takes 'якщо́', and the other clause is an imperative. 'Ві́льний' agrees with the friend: 'ві́льна' for a woman.
